paragraph.text: rights protect those who can be harmed, not those who can fulfill obligations. Confusing the two strips protection from babies, people with profound cognitive disabilities and anyone unable to reciprocate. And even those who accept the premise don't reach the conclusion: lacking rights, in the strict legal sense, doesn't authorize causing suffering.
"Animals have no duties, don't pay taxes, don't obey any law. So they can't have rights."
The classic formulation is Carl Cohen's, in a 1986 article in the
defending the use of animals in research:
Rights arise, and can only be defended, among beings who make, or can make, moral claims on one another.
Animals lack the capacity to understand and apply moral rules.
So animals have no rights, and in Cohen's words, "they can have none".
Those without rights may be used, subject to any duties of kindness.

Cohen anticipates the objection from humans lacking this capacity and replies that the capacity for moral judgment "is not a test to be administered to human beings one by one", because "the issue is one of kind". That way out is examined in chapter A18.

The same structure appears in contractualism: morality would be an agreement among rational agents, and only parties to the agreement would be protected by it. It's worth noting that John Rawls, although he excluded animals from the domain of justice, held that we have duties of compassion and humanity toward them.
fails at P1, which confuses who makes rules with whom the rules protect, at P2, which is partly false, and at P3, which doesn't follow: lacking legal rights isn't the same as moral permission.
"When the cow signs the constitution, we'll talk."
"Are you going to prosecute a shark for murder?"
"Rights exist only among beings able to make moral claims on one another." (Cohen)
"Morality is an agreement among those who can understand and follow rules."
"They aren't part of our moral community."

A newborn baby doesn't know what a rule is, doesn't help anyone and doesn't return favors. Even so, everyone agrees no one may hurt a baby. That shows something important: being protected isn't a prize you earn by fulfilling obligations. It's what is owed to those who can be hurt. Animals work the same way.
Two different things are being mixed up here.
are those who can have duties;

are those who can be harmed. Think of babies, people with advanced dementia and people in a coma: they're patients without being agents, and they don't lose protection for that. Our whole legal system works this way, with guardians representing those who can't claim anything. And if you also think we shouldn't be cruel to animals, as even those who deny them rights usually admit, that duty only makes sense if what happens to them matters.
"Does a baby have duties? Then why does it have rights?"
The argument lives on a conceptual confusion that moral philosophy resolved long ago.
Someone who can have duties and be held responsible
Someone who can be harmed or benefited
Babies, people with dementia, people in a coma, animals
Every moral agent is also a patient, but not every patient is an agent. Argument A21 demands of the patient the credentials of the agent. It's like refusing medical care to anyone who isn't a doctor.

There's also a leap between C1 and C2. Even if animals had no rights in the strict legal sense, it doesn't follow that we may do whatever we like with them. A consequentialist ethics doesn't even need the language of rights: avoidable suffering is enough to give a moral reason against it.

Newborns, people with profound intellectual disabilities and people in a coma have no duties and can't make claims. By P1's criterion, they'd have no rights. Almost no one accepts that, which is enough to reject the premise.

text.bold: 2. The law itself works this way.

paragraph.text: Guardianship exists precisely to represent those who can't make claims. Future generations, who can't reciprocate anything or take part in any agreement, appear in constitutions and environmental treaties as owed consideration. Inability to complain has never been an obstacle to legal protection.

text.bold: 3. The "it's a matter of kind" way out is circular.

paragraph.text: Cohen answers the human cases by saying moral capacity characterizes the species, not each individual. But that means judging someone by what other members of their species have, which is exactly the point in dispute. If we applied the same reasoning to intelligence, we'd say a baby can do algebra because adult humans can. Chapter A18 deals with this in detail.

Animals cooperate, return favors and punish cheating. Vampire bats share food with those who have fed them before, in a pattern of reciprocity documented by Wilkinson (1984). This doesn't make reciprocity a moral criterion, and the book doesn't want to fall into that trap. It only shows that the premise describes animals poorly.

Rawls excluded animals from the domain of justice, but affirmed duties of compassion and humanity toward them. Cohen defends their use in research and still recognizes human obligations of kindness. Conclusion C2, "so we may use them as we please", isn't supported even by the argument's own authors.

text.bold: 6. The law has already begun to move.

paragraph.text: In January 2022, Ecuador's Constitutional Court ruled, in the case of the monkey Estrellita, that individual animals are subjects of rights protected by the rights of nature, and ordered the state to produce specific legislation. In the United Kingdom, the sentience law came to recognize cephalopods and decapods. None of this required animals to take on duties.

text.bold: 7. Those who receive care needn't be able to give it.

paragraph.text: Requiring that someone be capable of acting morally in order to be considered is like requiring a patient to be a doctor in order to be treated. The beneficiaries of an activity needn't be able to perform it. See

text.link: Questão de Ética, vol. I, ch. 10

text.bold: 8. The cooperation version includes animals instead of excluding them.

paragraph.text: One variant speaks not of duties but of contribution. For John Rawls, justice governs a scheme of cooperation in which no one should gain from others' labor without doing their fair share, so only those who contribute would be entitled to what it distributes. The political philosopher Alasdair Cochrane notes that by this criterion many animals would have to be included: those on farms, in laboratories, in zoos and in homes are part of how society functions (Cochrane, 2010, pp. 55–57). Their contribution isn't chosen, and often costs them their lives; but that makes the exclusion worse, not better. And the criterion still leaves out humans who don't contribute, as Tom Regan points out about babies, who neither understand nor respect rights and still have them (Cochrane, 2010, p. 46). See also A25.

text.bold: 9. Reciprocity would make even the consideration of humans indirect.

paragraph.text: If we only owe something to those who cooperate or reciprocate, a gravely ill child who will never be able to contribute would only count for what they consume or for what others feel about them. Saying we care for the child because they buy medicine would be monstrous. And a contract made without anyone knowing whether they'd be born human or animal, as the philosopher Mark Rowlands (1998) proposes, would reject the reciprocity requirement, because anyone could turn out to be the one who can't reciprocate (Cunha, 2022, p. 213).

text.bold: 10. The "capacity" version is no longer reciprocity.

paragraph.text: To avoid excluding babies, some defenders of reciprocity say it is enough to have, or to come to have, the capacity to take part in agreements. Peter Singer notes, in

, that this version abandons the very idea that supported it: future generations, for instance, can never give anything back to those alive today, even if they come to have that capacity. If reciprocity is no longer required, it remains to be explained why morality should be limited to those capable of making agreements that will never be made (ch. 3). Chapter A23 brings Singer's other counterexamples.

text.bold: 11. The leap from C1 to C2 has a name: denying the antecedent.

paragraph.text: Reconstructed, the final step goes like this: "if animals have rights, harming them is wrong; they have no rights; so harming them is permitted". This is an invalid form,

text.link: denying the antecedent

paragraph.text: : from "if A, then B" and "not A" you can't conclude "not B". The philosopher Nathan Nobis shows the flaw with an argument of the same form: if you were a professional basketball player, you'd be over a foot tall; you aren't a professional basketball player; so you aren't over a foot tall. The premises are true and the conclusion is false (

, 2016, p. 41). In the same way, causing harm can be wrong for other reasons, such as the pain inflicted or the life taken, even if it violates no right. That's why Nobis proposes that the central question be whether a use is permissible, not whether animals "have rights" (pp. 9–10). It's a proposal for clarity, not a consensus: authors such as Tom Regan and Gary Francione argue that the language of rights is indispensable to protect each individual against aggregate calculations.

text.bold: 12. From each according to ability, to each according to need.

paragraph.text: The maxim became known through Karl Marx's

(1875), but it is older: the closest wording comes from the French socialist Louis Blanc, around 1850, and the idea echoes the Acts of the Apostles, where goods were shared according to each one's need. Marx used it for the distribution of goods; here it serves as an analogy, because it separates two things the argument mixes up. From each, duties are asked according to what they can do, and to each, consideration is given according to what they need. That is why duties are not demanded of babies, of people with profound cognitive disabilities or of animals, and they are not left unprotected for that reason: they need not to suffer, to eat, to have shelter and to live, even without being able to give anything back.

When people talk about animal rights, it is worth asking which rights are meant. Negative rights ask others to refrain: not to kill, not to imprison, not to hurt. Positive rights ask others to do something: to rescue, to feed, to care. What veganism asks is mostly of the first kind, to stop causing harm, and that does not require the animal to give anything back. Positive duties come up in other debates, such as

(d) The strongest counter-reply: the moral community
The strongest version doesn't say animal suffering is irrelevant. It says

There's an important truth embedded here. Animals aren't moral agents: they can't be held responsible, tried or punished, and it would be absurd to prosecute a lion for killing a gazelle. Reciprocity also explains well the historical origin of many norms, and the word "right", in the strict legal sense, involves institutions, representation and procedures that need careful design when the holder can't speak for themselves.

But none of this supports the conclusion. The asymmetry between us and them is exactly why the responsibility is ours. Only one side of this relationship can deliberate about what it does, and that side is us.
